extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students learning algebraic number theory (readers of Evan Chen's Napkin notes / Math 129)
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter giving definitions, lemmas, and proofs around class groups, the discriminant and signature of number fields, the canonical embedding, Minkowski's theorem and the Minkowski bound, and applications (finiteness of class group, class number computations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the class group (Cl_K = J_K / P_K)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let JK denote the multiplicative group of fractional ideals of O_K and PK the subgroup of principal fractional ideals (those of the form (x)=xO_K for x∈K). The class group Cl_K is defined as the quotient JK / PK. Equivalently: nonzero fractional ideals modulo scaling by constants in K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The elements (classes) measure how far O_K is from being a PID: O_K is a PID iff Cl_K is trivial. Classes can be thought of as shapes: two ideals are in the same class iff they are isomorphic as O_K-modules (or differ by multiplication by an element of K).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for fractional ideal in a Dedekind domain
rubrics_metrics.description: J is a fractional ideal of A (a Dedekind domain with fraction field K) iff (i) J is closed under addition and multiplication by elements of A, and (ii) J is finitely generated as an abelian group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More succinctly: J is a fractional ideal ⇐⇒ J is a finitely generated A-module. (This is Problem 55D.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fermat's little theorem for prime ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is a prime ideal in O_K then for α ∈ O_K one has α^{N(p)} ≡ α (mod p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the analogue of Fermat's little theorem in residue fields O_K/p which have size N(p). (Stated as Problem 55C.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminant of a number field (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If α1, …, αn is a Z-basis of O_K and σ1, …, σn are the embeddings K→C, the discriminant of K is defined by Δ_K := det[σ_i(α_j)]^2 (i.e. the square of the determinant of the matrix of embeddings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This determinant (squared as written) does not depend on the choice of Z-basis. The discriminant is an integer; for quadratic fields explicit formulae in terms of d (mod 4) are given in exercises and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature of a number field (r1,r2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a number field K of degree n, r1 is the number of real embeddings and r2 the number of pairs of complex embeddings. The signature is (r1,r2) with r1 + 2r2 = n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embeddings are ordered so the first r1 are real and the remaining occur in conjugate pairs. The canonical embedding uses this ordering to map K into R^{r1}×C^{r2} and then via τ into R^n by splitting complex parts into real and imaginary coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical embedding ι: K → R^{r1}×C^{r2} and τ: R^{r1}×C^{r2} → R^n
rubrics_metrics.description: The canonical embedding ι sends α to the tuple (σ1(α), …, σ_{r1}(α), σ_{r1+1}(α), …, σ_{r1+r2}(α)). The map τ breaks each complex coordinate into its real and imaginary parts to produce an element of R^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The composition τ∘ι is used to view O_K (and ideals) as lattices in R^n and to apply geometric arguments (volumes, Minkowski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mesh (covolume) of O_K as a lattice
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the canonical embedding (and τ to R^n) the image of O_K is a lattice L in R^n whose mesh (covolume) equals 2^{-r2}·√|Δ_K|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Lemma 56.3.6. The mesh is the hypervolume of a fundamental parallelepiped; authors often call it the volume, but here 'mesh' denotes that quantity. (Problem 56D asks to show this relation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mesh of the image lattice of an ideal a
rubrics_metrics.description: If a ⊆ O_K is a nonzero ideal with norm N(a) = |O_K/a|, then its image La under the canonical embedding is a lattice whose mesh equals N(a) times the mesh of L: mesh(La) = N(a)·2^{-r2}·√|Δ_K|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Lemma 56.3.7. Intuitively La contains only 1/N(a) of the points of L, so the fundamental region has N(a) times larger volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minkowski's theorem (geometry of numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let S ⊆ R^n be convex, centrally symmetric (x∈S ⇔ −x∈S) and containing 0. Let L be a lattice with mesh d. If (a) vol(S) > 2^n d, or (b) vol(S) = 2^n d and S is compact, then S contains a nonzero lattice point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof for (a) uses a pigeonhole-area argument by covering R^n with translations; (b) follows by approximating S by (1+ε)S and taking a limiting point. This theorem is the geometric core used to produce small-norm elements in ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the trap box S (mousetrap)
rubrics_metrics.description: For M>0 define S ⊆ R^{r1}×C^{r2} to be the set of points (x1,…,x_{r1}, z1,…,z_{r2}) satisfying Σ_{i=1}^{r1} |x_i| + 2·Σ_{j=1}^{r2} |z_j| ≤ M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of S as a 'mousetrap' tuned so that any nonzero α∈a lying in S must have small norm; choose M so that vol(S) is large enough to apply Minkowski to the lattice La.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of the mousetrap: AM–GM bound on the norm
rubrics_metrics.description: If α∈O_K has τ(ι(α)) ∈ S (the trap box), then N_{K/Q}(α) = Π_i |σ_i(α)| ≤ (M/n)^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Lemma 56.5.2. The inequality is obtained by comparing the product of the |σ_i(α)| with the arithmetic mean of the |σ_i(α)| using AM–GM and the defining inequality of S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume formula for the box S under τ
rubrics_metrics.description: The image τ(S) ⊆ R^n is convex, centrally symmetric and has volume vol(τ(S)) = 2^{r1}·(π/2)^{r2}·M^n / n! .
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Lemma 56.5.3. For sanity-checks the formula matches the 2D (r1=2,r2=0) and complex (r1=0,r2=1) case computations. The constants 2^{r1} and (π/2)^{r2} come from the shapes used for complex coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minkowski bound (existence of small-norm element in an ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a⊆O_K be any nonzero ideal. There exists 0≠α∈a such that |N_{K/Q}(α)| ≤ (n!/n^n)·(4/π)^{r2}·√|Δ_K|·N(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Theorem 56.6.1. Proof: choose M so that vol(τ(S)) = 2^n·mesh(La) and apply Minkowski to get nonzero α∈a with τ(ι(α))∈S, then use the mousetrap lemma to bound the norm. The displayed constant is the standard Minkowski constant and is often denoted in applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Minkowski constant M_K used to bound norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Define M_K := (n!/n^n)·(4/π)^{r2}·√|Δ_K| (a constant depending only on K). Then for any ideal a there exists α∈a with |N(α)| ≤ M_K·N(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constant is used to show every ideal class contains an integral ideal of norm ≤ M_K, which is the key to finiteness of the class group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finiteness of the class group (strategy via Minkowski bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the Minkowski bound M_K, every ideal class contains an integral ideal b with N(b) ≤ M_K. There are only finitely many integral ideals with norm ≤ M_K, hence Cl_K is finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The constructive proof proceeds by enumerating rational primes p ≤ M_K, factoring (p) in O_K, and then checking combinations of prime-ideal factors (the 'cherry tree' metaphor) whose norms multiply to ≤ M_K; only finitely many choices exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical computation method for class numbers using MK
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute Cl_K (or show it is trivial), compute MK and then consider rational primes p up to MK: factor x mod p minimal polynomials to determine factorization of (p); combine prime-ideal factors whose norms ≤ MK and check if resulting ideals are principal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for Q(i) MK<2 gives trivial class group; for Q(√−67) MK≈5.2 so only primes 2,3,5 need factoring, leading to conclusion Cl trivial in that example. Use Theorem 55.5.4 (polynomial reduction mod p) to determine splitting behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: ideals divide their norms
rubrics_metrics.description: If b is an integral ideal with N(b)=n then b‖(n) (i.e. b divides the principal ideal (n)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: n = |O_K/b|, so n·α ≡ 0 (mod b) for all α∈O_K, hence (n) ⊆ b. This lemma is used to restrict which rational primes can appear in the factorization of small-norm ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: deducing (p) is prime or splits from reduction of minimal polynomial
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the factorization of the ideal (p), reduce the minimal polynomial of an algebraic integer θ (generating O_K or a subring) modulo p: irreducible reduction implies (p) is prime; factorization pattern corresponds to splitting of (p) into prime ideals with norms equal to p^{f} where f are residual degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used repeatedly in examples (e.g., determining that (2),(3),(5) are prime in Q(√−67) by testing x^2 − x + 17 mod p). The textbook references Theorem 55.5.4 for the factoring algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dirichlet's unit theorem (structure of units)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let µ(O_K) be the finite group of roots of unity in K. If K has signature (r1,r2) set s = r1 + r2 − 1. Then there exist fundamental units u1,…,u_s such that every unit α∈O_K^× can be uniquely written as α = ω·u1^{n1}·...·u_s^{n_s} with ω∈µ(O_K) and n_i∈Z. Equivalently O_K^× ≅ µ(O_K) × Z^{r1+r2−1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem gives the full description of the multiplicative unit group and explains why real quadratic fields have infinite unit rank while imaginary quadratic fields have only roots of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof/strategy templates and exercises (how to show OK is free of rank n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three proof strategies are provided to prove O_K is a free Z-module of rank n: (i) compare O_K to a lattice spanned by a Q-basis and use discriminant/mesh arguments; (ii) use the dual lattice built from trace pairings; (iii) show non-freeness would contradict discreteness and continuity of the norm via Minkowski-type arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are procedural templates and exercises (56.9.i–iii, exercises) that guide how to produce rigorous proofs that O_K is a free Z-module. They include explicit computational devices (determinant d = det[Tr(α_i α_j)], dual lattice S, and mesh-decrease arguments).
